questions.problem:
$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}^{3}$ is defined as 

$$
⟨x,y⟩={x}_{1}{y}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{y}_{2}+2{x}_{3}{y}_{3},
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${v}_{2}⊥̸{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{2}⟩ & =(1)(4)+2(1)(-1)+2(-1)(1) \\  & =4-2-2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{2}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false since 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{2},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(4)(0)+2(-1)(1)+2(1)(1) \\  & =0-2+2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{2}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, computing the inner product $⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩$, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{v}_{1},{v}_{3}⟩ & =(1)(0)+2(1)(1)+2(-1)(1) \\  & =0+2-2 \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${v}_{1}⊥{v}_{3}$ with respect to the given inner product.
As a result, the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem:
Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)={t}^{2},\,{f}_{2}(t)={t}^{3},\,{f}_{3}(t)=t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-1,1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

*Hint: $⟨{f}_{1},{f}_{3}⟩=0.$*
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨{t}^{2},{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{5}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{6}}{6}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{{1}^{6}}{6}-\frac{(-1)^{6}}{6} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨{t}^{3},t⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{3}\cdot t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}-\frac{(-1)^{5}}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{2}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,{f}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{f}_{3}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi /2,\pi /2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ differentiating we have $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$ Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{2}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{2}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

Consider the following set of functions:

$$
{f}_{1}(t)={e}^{t},\,{f}_{2}(t)=t{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t},\,{f}_{3}(t)={e}^{-t}
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space $C[0,2]$ of continuous functions over $[0,2]$ is defined as 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t,
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨{e}^{t},t{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}(t{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-t){|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-2-(0-0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨{e}^{t},{e}^{-t}⟩ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =t{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${f}_{1}(t)⊥̸{f}_{3}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=2t+1,\,{p}_{2}(t)=3t,\,{p}_{3}(t)=t+1.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(0)q(0)+p(-1)q(-1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t+1,3t⟩ \\  & =(2t+1){|}_{0}\cdot (3t){|}_{0}+(2t+1){|}_{-1}\cdot (3t){|}_{-1} \\  & =(2(0)+1)\cdot (3(0))+(2(-1)+1)\cdot (3(-1)) \\  & =3\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨3t,t+1⟩ \\  & =(3t){|}_{0}\cdot (t+1){|}_{0}+(3t){|}_{-1}\cdot (t+1){|}_{-1} \\  & =(3(0))\cdot (0+1)+(3(-1))\cdot ((-1)+1) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Since ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{2}(t),$ the set $S$ is *not* orthogonal.
